channel.title: The Dig — Software stack: compilers and pulse level
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Software stack: compilers and pulse level preset. Today's ranked reading list collects five relevance-3 skims at the application and tooling edge of quantum computing: 2611.08151 on an ML surrogate for hybrid quantum Monte Carlo, 2611.08220 on differential testing for quantum software stacks, 2611.09873 on trajectory-dependent decoherence and leakage in shuttled multi-spin qubits, 2611.09659 on an OpenQASM3-to-QuEST compiler and HPC-quantum offload model, and 2611.09779 on differentiable digital twins for calibration and characterization of neutral-atom and trapped-ion systems; together they inform workflow acceleration, compiler validation, scaling theory, HPC integration, and calibration methodology, though none directly addresses operation or benchmarking of the current static 16-qubit spin-qubit QPU. item.title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
item.description:
Skim new method — Differential testing framework finds 6 instability sources across Qiskit, Cirq, and Pyquil (4 crash bugs, 2 root causes explaining 25 of 29 hardware divergences) while static circuit filtering reduces backend runs by 66%.

Grade 0.555 · 3.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “OpenQASM 3: A Broader and Deeper Quantum Assembly Language”

Figure

Equivalent circuits and resulting measurement outcome probability distributions on ibmq_yorktown, showing distribution divergence caused by 18 idle moments on qubit 4.

Asks

How to differentially test quantum software stacks across compilers, simulators, and hardware despite probabilistic outputs and severe execution costs?

But

Evaluated on at most 5 qubits without quantum error correction; total fuzzing run time capped at seven days.

Tools

QDiff · semantics-preserving source transformation · Kolmogorov-Smirnov test · cross entropy · L1 norm closeness testing

Code. https://github.com/wjy99-c/QDiff

Abstract

Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy

arxave:action.title: Prototype QDiff-style differential testing for our QSS

item.arxave:action: Build a small harness that applies semantics-preserving source transformations to OpenQASM circuits, runs them through our transpiler/simulator and a reference stack, and compares output distributions with KS/cross-entropy to catch compiler bugs before deployment.

arxave:action.title: Adapt circuit filtering to spin-qubit noise parameters

item.arxave:action: Use our measured T1, two-qubit gate error, and depth estimates to decide which generated circuits are worth executing on hardware, following QDiff's static filtering idea.

arxave:action.title: Ask authors about pulse-level and calibration coverage

item.arxave:action: Ask whether QDiff's equivalence checking can be extended to pulse-level APIs and calibration-state queries, since those are part of our operating requirements.
